name: National Bowl
text: Your train passes near the National Bowl, on the train's {side}, an open-air arena made from an old clay pit for brick-making. It opened in 1979; Queen played here in 1982, and Michael Jackson drew 60,000 fans on each of three nights.

name: Concrete Cows
text: Your train passes near the Concrete Cows, on the train's {side}, the replicas by the line at Bancroft of Liz Leyh's three cows and three calves of 1978. The originals, made from scrap and skinned with concrete, are now at Milton Keynes Museum.

name: Linslade Tunnel
text: Your train runs through Linslade Tunnel, whose three bores are the only tunnel on the London and Birmingham Railway built on a bend: local landowners refused to let the line pass closer to Leighton Buzzard. The first bore opened in 1837.

name: St Martin's Church, Fenny Stratford
text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church in Fenny Stratford, on the train's {side}, built by Browne Willis, its first stone laid on St Martin's Day 1724. Every St Martin's Day, November 11th, the Fenny Poppers, six small ceremonial cannon, are fired with blank charges at noon, 2pm and 4pm.

name: Magiovinium
text: Your train passes near the site of Magiovinium, on the train's {side}, a Roman town and fort at Dropshot Farm, at the edge of Fenny Stratford. Two hoards of Roman silver coins were found at or near the site, in 1967 and 1987.

name: Red Bull Racing
text: Your train passes near the factory of Red Bull Racing, on the train's {side}, the Formula One team based in Milton Keynes since 2004. It won the Constructors' Championship four years running from 2010, with Sebastian Vettel, and again in 2022 and 2023.

name: Bridego Bridge
text: Your train crosses Bridego Bridge, now officially Mentmore Bridge, where in August 1963 the Great Train Robbers stopped a Royal Mail train from Glasgow to London and escaped with more than £2.6 million. Most of the money was never found.

name: Tring Cutting
text: Your train runs through Tring Cutting, two and a half miles long and up to 60 feet deep, on the boundary of Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire. It was dug for the London and Birmingham Railway, opened in 1837, whose engineer, Robert Stephenson, was determined to keep its gradients as gentle as possible.

name: Shanklin
text: Your train runs into Shanklin, whose town is on the train's {side}, a seaside resort known for its Old Village and Shanklin Chine, a wooded ravine. The poet John Keats lodged in the High Street in the summer of 1819.

name: Sandown Barrack Battery
text: Your train passes near Sandown Barrack Battery, on the train's {side}, one of the Palmerston Forts built to defend the Isle of Wight against a feared French invasion. It was built between 1861 and 1863 for £6,233.

name: Brading Roman Villa
text: Your train passes near Brading Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, found in 1879 when a farmer making holes for a sheep pen struck a mosaic floor. The villa grew around three sides of a courtyard, and its mosaics are on show under a cover building.

name: Nunwell House
text: Your train passes near Nunwell House, on the train's {side}, home of the Oglander family for centuries. Sir John Oglander, a Royalist, hosted Charles I here on the King's last night of freedom.

name: Smallbrook Junction station
text: Smallbrook Junction station, at one end of this stretch, can't be reached except by train: it exists only for changing trains between Island Line and the Isle of Wight Steam Railway. It opened in 1991.

name: Royal Victoria Arcade
text: Your train passes near the Royal Victoria Arcade in Ryde, on the train's {side}, built in 1835 and 1836 and one of the first purpose-built shopping centres. It was named after Princess Victoria, later Queen Victoria, who had stayed at nearby Norris Castle.

name: Ryde Pier
text: Your train runs along Ryde Pier, the world's oldest seaside pleasure pier, opened in 1814. Before it was built, passengers were carried ashore on a porter's back and might have to walk up to half a mile across wet sand.

name: Shepperton station
text: Shepperton station, at one end of this stretch, is the terminus of a branch that opened in 1864. It was first meant to carry on to the River Thames by Chertsey Bridge, but that plan was dropped in 1862.

name: Upper Halliford station
text: Upper Halliford station, at one end of this stretch, opened as a halt in 1944 for a wartime factory of the British Thermostat Company that made munitions. Its second platform followed in 1946.

name: Kempton Park
text: Your train passes Kempton Park, on the train's {side}, first enclosed as a royal park in 1246; Henry VIII later hunted here. It is now home to Kempton Park Racecourse and a nature reserve.

name: Kempton Park Steam Engines
text: Your train passes near the Kempton Park waterworks, on the train's {side}, home to two triple-expansion steam engines of the late 1920s that each weigh more than 800 tons. One, the Sir William Prescott, still runs: the largest working engine of its kind in the world.

name: Tattenham Corner
text: Your train passes near Tattenham Corner, on the train's {side}, the sharp bend at the top of Epsom Racecourse and the last before the home straight of the Derby. Queen Elizabeth II used to arrive at the station by Royal Train on race days.

name: Tadworth Court
text: Your train passes near Tadworth Court, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed house built in 1700 in the Queen Anne style for Leonard Wessels, lord of the manor of Banstead. It is now home to The Children's Trust, a charity for disabled children.

name: Fames Rough
text: Your train passes near Fames Rough, on the train's {side}, a Surrey Wildlife Trust reserve on the Chipstead Downs. Part of its grassland is ploughed now and then to give a home to three very rare plants of arable fields, among them ground pine.

name: Woodmansterne station
text: Woodmansterne station, at one end of this stretch, isn't in Woodmansterne: the village lies across the Greater London boundary in Surrey, while the station serves the western side of Coulsdon.

name: Epsom College
text: Your train passes near Epsom College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1853 as the Royal Medical Benevolent College, to house pensioned doctors and to educate the sons of poor or deceased doctors.

name: Gally Hills, Banstead Downs
text: Your train passes near the Gally Hills on Banstead Downs, on the train's {side}, where Saxon burial mounds survive. Bronze Age axes and Iron Age and Roman pottery have also been found on the downs.

name: Farthing Downs
text: Your train passes near Farthing Downs, on the train's {side}, the largest area of semi-natural downland left in Greater London, owned by the City of London Corporation. Early medieval burial mounds survive at its north end.

name: East Surrey Hospital
text: Your train passes near East Surrey Hospital, on the train's {side}, which began as Reigate Cottage Hospital in 1866. The present hospital opened in 1981 and was formally opened by Margaret Thatcher in 1984.

name: Archway Theatre
text: Your train passes the Archway Theatre in Horley, on the train's {side}, an amateur theatre under the railway arches of the Victoria Road bridge, built in 1909. It has a 95-seat main auditorium and stages ten main productions a year.

name: RAF Kenley
text: Your train passes near the old airfield of RAF Kenley, on the train's {side}, one of the three RAF stations given the defence of London in the Battle of Britain. Pens built to shelter its fighters still survive.

name: Caterham Cars
text: Your train passes the former home of Caterham Cars, on the train's {side}, beside Caterham station. The firm bought the rights to the Lotus Seven in 1973 and still makes the Caterham Seven; its factory was in Caterham until 1987 and its showroom here until 2013.

name: Woldingham station
text: Woldingham station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1885 as Marden Park, named after the nearby manor, a year after the line itself. It was renamed Woldingham in 1894.

name: Oxted Tunnel
text: Your train runs through Oxted Tunnel, more than a mile long. It was dug in the 1860s, but work on the line stopped in 1869 and it did not open until 1884.

name: Limpsfield Tunnel
text: Your train runs through Limpsfield Tunnel, 551 yards long, at the southern end of Oxted station. The line through it opened in 1884.

name: St Peter and St Paul's Church, Lingfield
text: Your train passes near the church of St Peter and St Paul in Lingfield, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in 1431. Its brasses and monuments, including the tomb of Reginald de Cobham, 1st Baron Cobham, are among the finest in England.

name: Lingfield Park Racecourse
text: Your train passes Lingfield Park Racecourse, on the train's {side}, best known for flat racing in winter on an all-weather Polytrack rather than turf. Lingfield station adjoins the course.

name: Queen Victoria Hospital
text: Your train passes near the Queen Victoria Hospital in East Grinstead, on the train's {side}, where in the Second World War Archibald McIndoe pioneered reconstructive surgery for badly burned airmen. His patients formed the Guinea Pig Club here in 1941.

name: Eden Valley Museum
text: Your train passes near the Eden Valley Museum in Edenbridge, on the train's {side}, in a medieval farmhouse. Its collections include cricket-ball making, and a needlework box made by a German prisoner of war that featured in the BBC's A History of the World in 100 Objects.

name: St Peter and St Paul's Church, Edenbridge
text: Your train passes near the church of St Peter and St Paul in Edenbridge, on the train's {side}, whose oldest walls date from the 11th or early 12th century. Inside is stained glass by Edward Burne-Jones.

name: Markbeech
text: Your train passes near Markbeech, on the train's {side}, a small village on the northern ridges of the High Weald, in the parish of Hever, whose castle was the childhood home of Anne Boleyn.

name: Cowden Meadow
text: Your train passes Cowden Meadow, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest whose grassland has not been cultivated for many years, so it keeps flowers such as quaking grass, oxeye daisy and pepper saxifrage.
